El metro nació de la Revolución Francesa: The metre was born of the French Revolution with a lovely idea: that the unit should not depend on any king's foot, but on the Earth itself. It was defined as the ten-millionth part of a quarter of the Earth's meridian. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, took seven years (1792-1799) to measure the arc between Dunkirk and Barcelona in the middle of a war, being arrested several times as suspects. Today the metre is defined by the speed of light, but its length is still the one they measured.

Escribir más cifras de las que se han me: Writing more digits than you measured is claiming something you do not know. A phone GPS is accurate to a few metres, so giving a coordinate to millimetre precision is inventing the last digits. In a laboratory, in an expert report or on a building site, the number of digits you write communicates how much confidence the measurement deserves, and that is why quality standards regulate it.

Este es el error más frecuente del tema:: This is the most frequent error in the topic: using the linear factor on areas or volumes.
This is a free error detector. If after rearranging a formula you end up with a speed equated to an acceleration, there is no need to check the arithmetic: you already know it is wrong. Physicists also use it to guess formulas: you can deduce how the period of a pendulum depends on its length without solving anything, just by demanding that the units add up. It costs ten seconds and saves whole afternoons.
Hasta aquí los números iban solos. En cu: Up to here the numbers went alone. As soon as they measure something they carry a unit attached, and that unit behaves like one more factor: it multiplies, it divides and it cancels. This topic teaches you to change units without going wrong, not to write more digits than you have measured, and to use units as a detector of half-remembered formulas.

Y aquí llega la herramienta más útil de: And here comes the most useful tool in the whole topic, the one that acts as a safety net: in an equality, both sides have to have the same dimensions. You cannot add metres to seconds nor equate an energy to a speed.
Y no hace falta ir a Marte. En 1983, un: And you do not have to go to Mars. In 1983 an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at 12,000 metres because the refuelling was worked out in pounds when the aircraft was working in kilos: they loaded less than half of what was needed and the crew had to land gliding, engineless, on an abandoned runway. Nobody died, and the aircraft went down in history as the Gimli Glider. Day to day, the same sum decides a drug dose by body weight, the electricity supply rating of a house or the concrete on a building site: writing the unit next to every number is the cheapest habit there is for not going wrong.
